title: The Friday sermon
hook: two sermons before the Friday prayer, listened to in silence

segments.voice: Yesterday, jama'ah: prayer in rows, together. Today the row sits down and listens.

Medina, a Friday. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is standing and speaking to the people. Then a noise from the edge of town: a trade caravan has arrived, with goods to buy and the clamor of a market day. A report in Sahih al-Bukhari says people got up and went, and only a few stayed seated. The Qur'an kept the moment. In Pickthall's translation: "But when they spy some merchandise or pastime they break away to it and leave thee standing." The caravans are smaller now. They fit in a pocket, and they buzz.
screen: `A FRIDAY IN MEDINA.` → `THE CARAVAN ARRIVES.` → `THEY LEAVE HIM STANDING.`

segments.voice: Khutbah means a sermon, an address. On Friday, the congregational prayer called jumu'ah is preceded by one; you met it in year two, with leave trade for a while. First, its shape. Ibn Umar reported that the Prophet gave two sermons on Friday and sat briefly between them. So the imam stands, speaks, sits a moment, stands again, speaks again, and only then the prayer begins. Second, the call. Eight days ago this path heard surah sixty-two's command to haste unto remembrance of Allah when the call is heard. In Pickthall's translation the verse goes on: "and leave your trading." The same surah that keeps the caravan story tells people, two verses earlier, to put the market down when the call comes. Third, the silence. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari says that if you tell the person beside you to be quiet while the imam is speaking, you yourself have spoken idly. Even the shush counts. You listen, and let the person beside you do their own listening. Fourth, what the silence is for. The congregation hears a person speak to them about this week, this city, these lives. Some of it lands, some doesn't. The command is the same either way: the market waits, the shush waits, the phone waits. The caravan story ends with a line that answers it, in Pickthall's words: "That which Allah hath is better than pastime and than merchandise."
screen: `TWO SERMONS, A SIT BETWEEN.` · `LEAVE YOUR TRADING.` · `EVEN THE SHUSH COUNTS.` · `THE MARKET WAITS.` · then, large: `BETTER THAN PASTIME AND THAN MERCHANDISE.`

segments.voice: Put your phone out of reach, or face-down and silent if this lesson is playing on it, and listen to the room: the hum of something electric, a car outside, your own breath, without naming or judging any of it. If you attend the Friday prayer, you can leave the phone off or in the car this week and give the khutbah your whole hearing. If you don't, give one person a conversation with no screen anywhere in it.
Khutbah. The sermon: on Friday, two addresses before the prayer, heard in a silence so full it leaves no room even for shushing. Today's word.
Your line: silence for the khutbah. The market, the shush and the phone can all wait. Back tomorrow, same hill.

howItsDone: Each Friday at midday, Muslims gather at the mosque for jumu'ah: the imam gives two sermons with a short sit between them, the congregation listens in silence, and then they pray together.

notes: Editor: day 1078 had already quoted the first half of 62:9, so the teach now names that and quotes only its continuation ('and leave your trading'); 'a few verses earlier' corrected to 'two verses earlier' (62:9 vs 62:11); cut the unsourced 'the part people repeat'; closing screen changed to a 62:11 line to avoid re-showing 1078's. Hook's 'standing and speaking' follows 62:11 ('leave thee standing') and reports placing the caravan during the sermon (e.g. Muslim 863), while Bukhari 936 has 'while we were praying'; Keeper to confirm.
Pickthall 62:9 and 62:11 quoted from memory; confirm exact wording (62:9 begins 'O ye who believe!'; 62:11 continues 'Say: That which Allah hath ...').

Bukhari 936 (Jabir: a caravan arrived during the Friday sermon and people left, all but twelve men; 62:11 revealed). The count 'twelve' is replaced by 'only a few stayed'; confirm the hadith number and whether the event was during the khutbah or the prayer (reports differ).
Bukhari 928 (two khutbahs with a sitting between) and 934 (saying 'be quiet' during the khutbah is laghw) paraphrased; confirm numbers.
'The Friday prayer is preceded by' the sermons, and the myth that it does not follow: confirm; Eid prayers (sermon after) are not mentioned to keep one idea.
'In the khutbah, the congregation hears a person speak to them ... about this week, this city' is the writer's framing of the sermon's purpose; confirm.
